# Lab: two sched tasks keep a promise

<!-- type: tutorial · level: 2 · topic: realtime -->

**Needs first:** [Run a talker](run-a-talker.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: chapter status -->
> **Status:** this chapter runs on [`nros-board-mps2-an385-freertos`](../reference/boards/mps2-an385-freertos.md): Verified in emulator (daily). From the board support registry; [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.
<!-- END GENERATED chapter status -->

A control loop makes a promise: it runs every period, and it is never so late
that the thing it controls notices. On a microcontroller that promise is
broken most often not by the loop itself but by something else on the same
processor that runs too long. In this lab you build that situation on
purpose: a 100 Hz control loop and a 10 Hz telemetry job whose every run takes
60 ms. You put both on one sched task and watch the loop miss its periods,
then give the loop a sched task of its own, at a higher priority, and watch it
keep its period while the telemetry job does exactly the same work.

The loop grades itself. Every 100 ticks it prints the longest gap between two
of its ticks, and after 1,000 ticks it prints how many of those ten windows
broke a 50 ms budget. At the end, `nros run` prints `10 windows, 0 late`.

The lab runs on the emulated MPS2-AN385 with FreeRTOS, in Rust, C or C++. It
uses a workspace of its own, beside the Tutorial's `sensor_ws`, and takes
about an hour, most of it reading.

## What a sched task is

An executor runs callbacks one at a time. When a timer is due, the executor
calls its callback, and it calls the next one only when that callback
returns. That is what makes a callback simple to write, since nothing else
in the same executor touches its state while it runs. It is also the
problem this lab is about: a callback that is due cannot start while another
one is still running.

A **sched task** is an RTOS task that runs part of the image's callbacks,
with a priority of its own. You decide which callbacks run where in two
steps:

1. In the node's code, put the callbacks in a named **callback group**.
2. In the bringup's `system.toml`, bind each group to a sched task with
   `group_tasks`, and give each sched task a `[tasks.<name>]` table, with
   its FreeRTOS priority in `[tasks.<name>.freertos]`.

The code never names a sched task or a priority, so the same node runs on
one task or on two, and on another RTOS, without a change. On FreeRTOS a
bigger number is more urgent, and a more urgent task that becomes ready
takes the processor from a less urgent one at once, in the middle of its
callback.

## Write the control loop

The loop runs every 10 ms. It does no control work; it only measures itself.
On each tick it reads a steady clock, keeps the longest gap since the
previous tick, and every 100 ticks prints that gap and whether it broke the
budget of 50 ms, five periods. Replace the talker's code:

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

```bash probe=2130 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/control_node/src/lib.rs <<'EOF'
//! A 100 Hz control loop that measures itself: the longest gap between
//! two of its ticks, judged against a 50 ms budget.

#![no_std]

use nros::{
    Callback, CallbackCtx, Component, DeclarativeNode, ExecutableNode, NodeContext, NodeOptions,
    NodeResult,
    TimerDuration,
};
use nros_log::{Logger, log_info};

static LOGGER: Logger = Logger::new("control_node");

/// Five periods: a tick later than this is late.
const BUDGET_US: u64 = 50_000;

pub struct Talker;

impl Component for Talker {
    const NAME: &'static str = "control_node";

    const ENTITY_BOUNDS: nros::EntityBounds = nros::EntityBounds::exact(0, 0, 0, 0, 0);

    fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
        nros_log::register_logger(&LOGGER);
        let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("control_node"))?;
        // Everything created after this line belongs to the group `ctrl`.
        node.callback_group("ctrl")?;
        let _timer =
            node.create_timer_for_callback_name("on_tick", TimerDuration::from_millis(10))?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

/// Ticks so far, the last tick's time, the window's longest gap, late windows.
pub struct Loop {
    ticks: u32,
    last_us: u64,
    worst_us: u64,
    late: u32,
}

impl ExecutableNode for Talker {
    type State = Loop;
    const HAS_TICK: bool = false;

    fn init() -> Self::State {
        Loop { ticks: 0, last_us: 0, worst_us: 0, late: 0 }
    }

    fn on_callback(s: &mut Self::State, callback: Callback<'_>, _ctx: &mut CallbackCtx<'_>) {
        if callback.as_str() != "on_tick" {
            return;
        }
        let now = nros::time::now_us();
        if s.ticks > 0 {
            s.worst_us = s.worst_us.max(now.saturating_sub(s.last_us));
        }
        s.last_us = now;
        s.ticks += 1;
        if s.ticks % 100 == 0 {
            let late = s.worst_us > BUDGET_US;
            if late {
                s.late += 1;
            }
            log_info!(
                &LOGGER,
                "ticks {}-{}: longest gap {} us ({})",
                s.ticks - 99,
                s.ticks,
                s.worst_us,
                if late { "late" } else { "on time" }
            );
            s.worst_us = 0;
            if s.ticks == 1000 {
                log_info!(&LOGGER, "10 windows, {} late", s.late);
            }
        }
    }
}

nros::node!(Talker);
EOF
```

#### C

```bash probe=2130 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/control_node/src/Talker.c <<'EOF'
// A 100 Hz control loop that measures itself: the longest gap between two
// of its ticks, judged against a 50 ms budget.

#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>

#include <rcl/rcl.h>
#include <rclc/executor.h>
#include <rclc/rclc.h>

// Five periods: a tick later than this is late.
#define BUDGET_NS (50LL * 1000000LL)

typedef struct {
    rcl_timer_t timer;
    int32_t ticks;
    int64_t worst_ns;
    int32_t late;
} control_t;

// `since_last` is rcl's `last_call_time`: nanoseconds since the previous call.
static void on_tick(rcl_timer_t* timer, int64_t since_last) {
    control_t* self = RCLC_CONTAINER_OF(timer, control_t, timer);
    if (self->ticks > 0 && since_last > self->worst_ns) {
        self->worst_ns = since_last;
    }
    self->ticks++;
    if (self->ticks % 100 == 0) {
        int late = self->worst_ns > BUDGET_NS;
        if (late) {
            self->late++;
        }
        printf("[control_node] ticks %d-%d: longest gap %lld us (%s)\n", (int)self->ticks - 99,
               (int)self->ticks, (long long)(self->worst_ns / 1000), late ? "late" : "on time");
        self->worst_ns = 0;
        if (self->ticks == 1000) {
            printf("[control_node] 10 windows, %d late\n", (int)self->late);
        }
    }
}

static rcl_ret_t control_configure(rcl_node_t* node, rclc_executor_t* executor, control_t* self) {
    (void)node;
    setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IOLBF, 0);
    self->ticks = 0;
    self->worst_ns = 0;
    self->late = 0;
    self->timer = rcl_get_zero_initialized_timer();
    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_timer_init_default(&self->timer, NULL, 10ULL * 1000000ULL, on_tick);
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) {
        return rc;
    }
    return rclc_executor_add_timer(executor, &self->timer);
}

RCLC_C_COMPONENT(control_t, control_configure)
EOF
```

#### C++

```bash probe=2130 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/control_node/include/control_node/Talker.hpp <<'EOF'
#pragma once

#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>

namespace control_node {

/// A 100 Hz control loop that measures itself: the longest gap between two
/// of its ticks, judged against a 50 ms budget.
class Talker {
    ::rclcpp::Timer timer_;
    ::rclcpp::Clock clock_{RCL_STEADY_TIME};
    int ticks_ = 0;
    int64_t last_ns_ = 0;
    int64_t worst_ns_ = 0;
    int late_ = 0;

    void on_tick();

  public:
    ::rclcpp::Result configure(::rclcpp::Node& node);
};

} // namespace control_node
EOF
cat > src/control_node/src/Talker.cpp <<'EOF'
#include "control_node/Talker.hpp"

#include <cstdio>

namespace control_node {

// Five periods: a tick later than this is late.
static const int64_t kBudgetNs = 50LL * 1000000LL;

void Talker::on_tick() {
    const int64_t now = clock_.now().nanoseconds();
    if (ticks_ > 0 && now - last_ns_ > worst_ns_) worst_ns_ = now - last_ns_;
    last_ns_ = now;
    ++ticks_;
    if (ticks_ % 100 == 0) {
        const bool late = worst_ns_ > kBudgetNs;
        if (late) ++late_;
        std::printf("[control_node] ticks %d-%d: longest gap %lld us (%s)\n", ticks_ - 99, ticks_,
                    (long long)(worst_ns_ / 1000), late ? "late" : "on time");
        worst_ns_ = 0;
        if (ticks_ == 1000) std::printf("[control_node] 10 windows, %d late\n", late_);
    }
}

::rclcpp::Result Talker::configure(::rclcpp::Node& node) {
    ::setvbuf(stdout, nullptr, _IONBF, 0);
    return node.create_wall_timer<Talker, &Talker::on_tick>(timer_, 10, this);
}

} // namespace control_node
EOF
```

<!-- /tabs -->


Three things to notice:

- **The callback group.** In Rust, `node.callback_group("ctrl")` puts
  everything the node creates after it, here the timer, in the group `ctrl`.
  In C and C++ the group is the package's, named in its `CMakeLists.txt`
  below.
- **The clock.** A gap is measured on a steady clock, one that never jumps
  when the wall time is set. Rust reads `nros::time::now_us()`; C gets the
  time since the previous call as the timer callback's second argument,
  rcl's `last_call_time`; C++ reads an `rclcpp::Clock` built on
  `RCL_STEADY_TIME`.
- **No publisher.** The loop prints to the console and publishes nothing,
  so the lab measures scheduling and nothing else.

## Write the telemetry job

The telemetry job runs every 100 ms and spends 60 ms of processor time each
time, standing in for real work such as compressing a log. Its callback
does not sleep or wait: it keeps the processor busy until 60 ms have passed,
which is what a long computation does.

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

```bash probe=2140 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/telemetry_node/src/lib.rs <<'EOF'
//! A 10 Hz telemetry job whose every run takes 60 ms of processor time.

#![no_std]

use nros::{
    Callback, CallbackCtx, Component, DeclarativeNode, ExecutableNode, NodeContext, NodeOptions,
    NodeResult,
    TimerDuration,
};

pub struct Talker;

impl Component for Talker {
    const NAME: &'static str = "telemetry_node";

    const ENTITY_BOUNDS: nros::EntityBounds = nros::EntityBounds::exact(0, 0, 0, 0, 0);

    fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
        let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("telemetry_node"))?;
        node.callback_group("telem")?;
        let _timer =
            node.create_timer_for_callback_name("on_tick", TimerDuration::from_millis(100))?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl ExecutableNode for Talker {
    type State = ();
    const HAS_TICK: bool = false;

    fn init() -> Self::State {}

    fn on_callback(_s: &mut Self::State, callback: Callback<'_>, _ctx: &mut CallbackCtx<'_>) {
        if callback.as_str() == "on_tick" {
            // Stand-in for real work: compress a log, format a report.
            let t0 = nros::time::now_us();
            while nros::time::now_us().saturating_sub(t0) < 60_000 {
                core::hint::spin_loop();
            }
        }
    }
}

nros::node!(Talker);
EOF
```

#### C

```bash probe=2140 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/telemetry_node/src/Talker.c <<'EOF'
// A 10 Hz telemetry job whose every run takes 60 ms of processor time.

#include <stdint.h>

#include <rcl/rcl.h>
#include <rclc/executor.h>
#include <rclc/rclc.h>

typedef struct {
    rcl_timer_t timer;
    rcl_clock_t clock;
} telemetry_t;

static void on_tick(rcl_timer_t* timer, int64_t since_last) {
    telemetry_t* self = RCLC_CONTAINER_OF(timer, telemetry_t, timer);
    (void)since_last;
    // Stand-in for real work: compress a log, format a report.
    int64_t t0 = 0;
    int64_t t = 0;
    rcl_clock_get_now(&self->clock, &t0);
    do {
        rcl_clock_get_now(&self->clock, &t);
    } while (t - t0 < 60LL * 1000000LL);
}

static rcl_ret_t telemetry_configure(rcl_node_t* node, rclc_executor_t* executor,
                                     telemetry_t* self) {
    (void)node;
    rcl_ret_t rc = rcl_clock_init(RCL_STEADY_TIME, &self->clock, NULL);
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) {
        return rc;
    }
    self->timer = rcl_get_zero_initialized_timer();
    rc = rclc_timer_init_default(&self->timer, NULL, 100ULL * 1000000ULL, on_tick);
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) {
        return rc;
    }
    return rclc_executor_add_timer(executor, &self->timer);
}

RCLC_C_COMPONENT(telemetry_t, telemetry_configure)
EOF
```

#### C++

```bash probe=2140 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/telemetry_node/include/telemetry_node/Talker.hpp <<'EOF'

/// A 10 Hz telemetry job whose every run takes 60 ms of processor time.

void Talker::on_tick() {
    // Stand-in for real work: compress a log, format a report.
    const int64_t t0 = clock_.now().nanoseconds();
    while (clock_.now().nanoseconds() - t0 < 60LL * 1000000LL) {
    }
}

::rclcpp::Result Talker::configure(::rclcpp::Node& node) {

}
```

## State what the nodes create

The scaffold wrote a contract for two talkers that publish on `/chatter`
once a second. The nodes now publish nothing and tick at 100 Hz and 10 Hz,
so replace it with one that says so:

```bash probe=2150 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/control_node_bringup/system.contract.yaml <<'EOF'
version: 1

nodes:
  control_node:
    params: {}
    paths:
      on_tick:
        trigger: { timer: { rate_hz: 100 } }
        output: []
  telemetry_node:
    params: {}
    paths:
      on_tick:
        trigger: { timer: { rate_hz: 10 } }
        output: []
EOF
```

Each node has a timer path with its rate and no output, and an empty
`params:`. The build sizes the image's callback table from these rows, so a
timer missing from the contract is a timer the image has no room for.

## One sched task

First put both groups on one sched task, `main`. Add the task to the
bringup's `system.toml`, and bind each node's group to it on its
`[[component]]` row:

```bash probe=2160 track=installed variant=qemu
cat >> src/control_node_bringup/system.toml <<'EOF'

[tasks.main]
spin_period = "10000us"
[tasks.main.freertos]
priority = 2
EOF
sed -i -e '/^pkg = "control_node"$/a group_tasks = { ctrl = "main" }' \
       -e '/^pkg = "telemetry_node"$/a group_tasks = { telem = "main" }' \
       src/control_node_bringup/system.toml
```

The two rows now read:

```toml
[[component]]
pkg = "control_node"
group_tasks = { ctrl = "main" }
class = "control_node::Talker"
name = "control_node"

[[component]]
pkg = "telemetry_node"
group_tasks = { telem = "main" }
class = "telemetry_node::Talker"
name = "telemetry_node"
```

`spin_period` is how long the sched task's executor may sleep when nothing
is due. Priority 2 is below the network stack's tasks, which this board runs
at 4; a sched task that outranked them would starve the transport it
depends on, and the build refuses one unless it says so.

Run it, and wait for the tenth window. The run takes about 40 seconds:

```bash probe=2170 probe-run=900 track=installed variant=qemu
nros run --expect '10 windows, 10 late'
```

```text probe-expect=2170 variant=qemu
10 windows, 10 late
```

Every window is late. The console shows why in its numbers:

```text
[WARN] nros: [    2.282421] contract violation: timer-overrun-runtime timer measured=5 declared=0
...
[INFO] control_node: [    5.287820] ticks 1-100: longest gap 189036 us (late)
[INFO] control_node: [    9.295950] ticks 101-200: longest gap 147774 us (late)
...
[INFO] control_node: [   40.610821] ticks 901-1000: longest gap 152845 us (late)
[INFO] control_node: [   40.613991] 10 windows, 10 late
```

That is a Rust project's console; a C or C++ project's gaps are about half
as long, 70 to 80 ms, and late all the same. Once every 100 ms the telemetry
callback takes the executor for 60 ms, and the loop's ticks that fall due in
that time cannot start until it returns. The loop's timer then fires once
and counts the periods it missed, rather than replaying them, which is what
the `timer-overrun-runtime` warnings report: activations the image dropped.
A thousand ticks at 10 ms should take ten seconds; they took four times as
long, because most of them never happened.

## Two sched tasks

Now give the loop a sched task of its own, `high`, at priority 3, above
`main` and still below the network stack. Only the loop's binding changes;
the telemetry job stays on `main`:

```bash probe=2180 track=installed variant=qemu
cat >> src/control_node_bringup/system.toml <<'EOF'

[tasks.high]
spin_period = "1000us"
[tasks.high.freertos]
priority = 3
EOF
sed -i 's/group_tasks = { ctrl = "main" }/group_tasks = { ctrl = "high" }/' \
    src/control_node_bringup/system.toml
```

Run it again:

```bash probe=2190 probe-run=900 track=installed variant=qemu
nros run --expect '10 windows, 0 late'
```

```text probe-expect=2190 variant=qemu
10 windows, 0 late
```

```text
[INFO] control_node: [    3.136740] ticks 1-100: longest gap 12420 us (on time)
...
[INFO] control_node: [   12.759645] ticks 901-1000: longest gap 21469 us (on time)
[INFO] control_node: [   12.766466] 10 windows, 0 late
```

The telemetry job still spends 60 ms of every 100. What changed is who waits.
When the loop's timer falls due, the `high` task becomes ready, FreeRTOS
takes the processor from the `main` task in the middle of the telemetry
callback, the loop runs its tick, and the telemetry callback resumes where
it was. A thousand ticks now take ten seconds of the board's time. A C or
C++ build prints the two tasks it made:

```text
codegen entry:   sched task high: priority 3 (authored)
codegen entry:   sched task main: priority 2 (authored)
```

## What the numbers do not say

The loop's longest gap, between 12 and 26 ms in these runs, is longer than
its 10 ms period even with a task of its own. That is the emulator's floor,
and it is the same with the telemetry job doing no work at all: the network
stack's tasks run above both sched tasks, and an emulated processor's time
advances in steps of its own. The lab's budget of five periods is set above
that floor so that the comparison is between the two schedules, not between
the emulator and a perfect clock.

On a real board the floor is lower, and its height is a property of that
board, measured there. What carries over is the shape of the result: on its
own sched task, the loop's worst case does not depend on how long the
telemetry job runs. On a shared one it does, and no budget holds once the
job grows.

## Change it

Predict each result before you run it, then check it against the console.

- **Make the job lighter, then heavier.** Change the telemetry job's 60 ms
  to 0, then to 90, and run the two-task setup each time. Does the loop's
  longest gap follow the job's length? Run the one-task setup at 90 ms: what
  does the loop's gap follow there?
- **Swap the priorities.** Give `high` priority 1, below `main`. The loop is
  alone on its task; is that enough?
- **Move the job instead.** Put `telem` on a new task at priority 1 and leave
  `ctrl` on `main`. Which property of the setup kept the loop on time: that
  it had a task to itself, or that its task outranked the job's?

## If it doesn't work

- **The build refuses a priority:** a sched task's priority must stay below
  the board's network stack (4 on this board). The refusal names the band.
- **Both runs print `0 late`:** check that the two `group_tasks` lines
  landed on the `[[component]]` rows, not elsewhere: `grep -n group_tasks
  src/control_node_bringup/system.toml`. A group that no row binds is not on
  `main`.
- **No `ticks` lines at all:** the loop's timer never ran. In C or C++, the
  `CALLBACK_GROUPS` line must sit inside `nano_ros_add_node(...)`, before
  `SOURCES`; in Rust, `callback_group` must come before the timer is
  created.
- **`nros run` stops before the tenth window:** with `--timeout`, give the
  one-task run about a minute; it takes four times as long as the other.

## What just happened

| Setup | Who waits | Loop's longest gap | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| one sched task, `main` | the loop, behind every 60 ms telemetry run | 70 to 190 ms | `10 windows, 10 late` |
| `ctrl` on `high` (3), `telem` on `main` (2) | the telemetry job, preempted mid-callback | 12 to 26 ms | `10 windows, 0 late` |

A callback group says which callbacks belong together, in the code. A sched
task says how urgent they are, in the bringup. Keeping the two apart is what
lets the same nodes run under either schedule: you changed one line of
`system.toml` between the runs, and no code.

## Design background

Sched tasks and their mapping onto RTOS tasks follow RFC-0015. How a sched
task's priority is checked against the board's own tasks follows RFC-0079.
